topic: Bayes' Theorem and the Logic of Independence
target_audience: Undergraduate students or advanced high school students

sections.title: Introduction: The Intuition of Independence
lecture_lines: Independence means one event doesn't affect another's probability.
A cat meowing doesn't change a coin flip's outcome.
We represent this visually using a probability square.
animations: Create a large unit square (#D3D3D3) representing the total probability 1.
Highlight a vertical strip 'Event A' (#ADD8E6) and a horizontal strip 'Event B' (#FFB6C1).
Highlight the intersection area (#00FF00) and label it 'Area = P(A) * P(B)' to show independence.

sections.title: Prerequisite: Conditional Probability & The Shrinking Universe
lecture_lines: Conditional probability looks at events within a restricted universe.
We imagine our sample space shrinking to event B.
We then find the probability of A within B.
animations: Display a large rectangle 'S' (#D3D3D3) with a sub-region 'B' (#FFB6C1).
Label the entire rectangle 'S' as the 'Universal Set' (#FFFFFF).
Scale the scene so the rectangle 'B' fills the screen, fading out the rest of 'S'.
Draw region 'A' (#ADD8E6) within 'B', highlighting the overlap 'A ∩ B' (#00FF00).
Display the formula P(A|B) = Area(A ∩ B) / Area(B) next to the graphic (#FFFFFF).

sections.title: The Core: Deriving Bayes' Theorem
lecture_lines: Bayes' Theorem allows us to flip conditional probabilities.
We start by relating intersections to conditional probabilities.
By setting these equal, we find a new relationship.
This formula helps us update beliefs with new evidence.
The result is the famous Bayes' Theorem formula.
animations: Display the equation P(A and B) = P(A|B) * P(B) in the center (#FFFFFF).
Below it, display the symmetric equation P(A and B) = P(B|A) * P(A) (#FFFFFF).
Animate an equals sign between P(A|B) * P(B) and P(B|A) * P(A), highlighting both terms in yellow (#FFFF00).
Fade out the shared P(A and B) part and move the right side terms to form a single equality.
Rearrange terms to show P(A|B) = [P(B|A)P(A)] / P(B), putting a bright box (#00FF00) around it.

sections.title: Step-by-Step Application: The Rare Dragon Test
lecture_lines: Consider a rare dragon and a 99% accurate detector.
Only one in a thousand creatures is a dragon.
False alarms from non-dragons can outweigh true results.
We calculate the total probability of a positive test.
Bayes shows the real chance is only nine percent.
animations: Display 'P(Dragon) = 0.001' (#FFD700) and 'P(No Dragon) = 0.999' (#FFFFFF).
Show 'P(+|Dragon) = 0.99' (#ADD8E6) and 'P(+|No Dragon) = 0.01' (#FFB6C1).
Flash the text 'If Alarm Sounds (+)...' (#FFFFFF) at the top.
Show the calculation: P(+) = (0.99 * 0.001) + (0.01 * 0.999) approx 0.011 (#FFFFFF).
Compute P(Dragon|+) = (0.99 * 0.001) / 0.011 approx 0.09, highlighted in green (#00FF00).

sections.title: Conclusion: Independence vs. Bayesian Updating
lecture_lines: Independence means new information doesn't change our beliefs.
Dependence allows us to update certainty using Bayes' Theorem.
Use these tools to master the logic of probability.
animations: Show the 'Probability Square' (#D3D3D3) on the left (Intersection = Product).
Show the 'Shrinking Universe' (#FFB6C1) on the right (Update based on evidence).
Display a summary label 'Master Your Logic' (#FFFFFF) as both graphics fade to a centered Bayes formula (#00FF00).
